Jim Cramer sends a strong signal to Nvidia stock investors

Nvidia has gone from Wall Street's favorite stock to one of its most heavily sold stocks in just a few weeks. Shares have dropped about 22% over the past month, and Wednesday's session was ugly. The stock closed at $186.24, down nearly 7% on the day, as a broad sell-off hit the chip sector hard. AMD fell more than 17% and Broadcom dropped more than 10%.

Jim Cramer, the host of CNBC's Mad Money, spent part of his Wednesday program making the case that now is the time to buy. His argument rests on valuation: "This is the cheapest multiple on Nvidia in about a decade. We're at 16.5 now." He said investors are writing off a company he believes remains the dominant force in artificial intelligence infrastructure, 24/7 Wall St. reported.

What sparked the Nvidia selloff

The slide started in late September. At that point, Nvidia's shares sat at about 17 times forward earnings, a level not seen since January 2015.

Also read: Jim Cramer sends clear signal on Apple and Palantir stock

The stock's 15-year average is roughly 30 times. The discount was real, but sellers kept coming anyway.

The trigger on Wednesday appears to have been a mix of concerns: worries about AI regulation, questions over whether hyperscalers will keep spending at the pace Nvidia needs, and rotation out of high-multiple tech names. The selloff was broad enough to drag down the entire chip sector, not just Nvidia.

Nvidia's fundamentals tell a different story

The business results themselves have been hard to fault. In its fiscal second quarter, Nvidia posted revenue of $96.2 billion, up sharply from a year earlier. Data center revenue came in at $89 billion, a 117% jump. Earnings of $2.22 a share beat the $2.09 consensus estimate. The company guided for fiscal third-quarter revenue of $108 billion, a figure that left some investors expecting more, according to Nvidia.

The company has also been using its cash aggressively. Nvidia repurchased about $39.8 billion worth of its own stock in the first half of fiscal 2027, and it still had $99 billion left on its buyback authorization at the end of the second quarter. Total buyback capacity, including a new tranche approved in late September, now stands at $235 billion, Cramer noted on X.

Related: Whirlpool delivers bad news to customers before Black Friday

Cash on the balance sheet stood at $56.6 billion. Supply commitments have more than doubled, from $119 billion to $279 billion, a sign that the company is locking in future production at scale. Revenue from the roughly 50 largest frontier AI labs alone accounts for about $50 billion of that pipeline, the Motley Fool reported.

title: AMD Stock Popped After Earnings, Then Gave It All Back. Is It a Buy Now?
detail:
AMD Stock Popped After Earnings, Then Gave It All Back. Is It a Buy Now?

^GSPC
NVDA

AMD (NASDAQ: AMD) reported third-quarter earnings on Nov. 3, and the stock rose sharply after hours, up around 8%. However, over the next day, the market was less and less impressed with the results, and AMD ended Nov. 4 up only about 1% -- less than the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) rose. So, what caused the market to change its mind after a strong reaction?

I think investors are looking at AMD as a whole, rather than just a single quarter.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

The reality is that AMD's stock has risen tremendously fast this year, far outpacing its business growth. This mismatch has vaulted AMD's stock into expensive territory, and that reality is apparently becoming clear to investors.

Image source: The Motley Fool.
AMD sees strong data center growth ahead

First, let's digest the quarter. AMD makes all types of computing units, ranging from data center GPUs to consumer hardware to embedded chip processors. However, the big cash cow is its data center business, which is growing rapidly. During Q3, AMD's data center business rose 97% year over year to $8.5 billion. However, this still represents a slowdown from the 107% growth seen in Q2. Furthermore, data centers are only a part of AMD's business. AMD's overall revenue totaled $13.4 billion, up 45% year over year. So, AMD is being held back by its other business units.

Looking ahead, AMD expects strong growth. It expects data center revenue to double year over year in 2027 -- indicating that its growth in this area will remain strong. That's great news for investors, as it suggests AMD's overall growth rate will likely increase. With its data center division growing faster than the company overall, it will start to make up an ever larger share of AMD's total. With it having a greater effect, AMD's overall growth rate will move closer to the data center unit's.

This is great news, but it's also required, as AMD's stock has a lot of future growth priced in.

AMD isn't a cheap stock

Right now, AMD is one of the more expensive stocks on the market.

AMD PE Ratio data by YCharts

Priced at 106 times trailing earnings, AMD's stock is expensive no matter how you slice it. The company needs to grow its way into a more reasonable valuation. One way AMD is doing this is by improving margins. Each quarter over the past few years, AMD's profit margins have trended up. However, they are starting to go a bit sideways.

Qualcomm (QCOM) stock gained 5.5% on Friday, November 6, 2026, while the S&P 500 rose 0.3%. The company issued no announcements, earnings reports or filings that day, and four of its five peers also finished higher. Separately, Reuters reported on Friday that Alphabet disclosed a Qualcomm stake worth $548 million. Friday's gain followed a 9.5% fall on Thursday, November 5, the day after Qualcomm reported its fiscal fourth-quarter results. So what changed for chip stocks, and for Qualcomm, between Thursday and Friday?

Qualcomm Rose As Chip Stocks Recovered From A Sell-Off

Qualcomm climbed on Friday as semiconductor shares bounced back from a sell-off. A Democratic sweep of Congress in Tuesday's midterm elections raised fears in the market of a slowdown in data center spending, and stocks sold off sharply on Thursday. Chip stocks were lower across the board that day. Qualcomm led the decline after its fourth-quarter results slightly beat estimates but came with light guidance. Stocks recovered some of those losses on Friday, with Nvidia, AMD and other chip manufacturers rebounding alongside Qualcomm.

A partial recovery isn't an all-clear. But a year after 21 sell-offs this sharp, the S&P 500 was higher 20 times.

These market fears reach Qualcomm because the company is building a data center business alongside its phone chips. On its November 4 call, management reiterated its $5 billion revenue target for data center in fiscal 2027. Management said most of that revenue is custom silicon for AI accelerators at two large cloud customers.

How Did Qualcomm Compare With Other Chip Makers?

Qualcomm rose more than three of the five chip makers on its peer list. Texas Instruments was the only company among the five to fall. Advanced Micro Devices posted the largest rise in the group, gaining 11.0%, while Intel also rose more than Qualcomm.

The wider technology sector advanced at a slower pace. XLK, the SPDR fund that tracks the sector, gained 1.5%, finishing well short of Qualcomm's rise. Qualcomm moved in step with its chip peers rather than on its own.

Qualcomm Stock Is Still Down Over Twelve Months

A rise of this size is not rare for Qualcomm. The stock recorded 11 sessions with a gain at least this large in the prior 365 days, and its most recent move of this magnitude in either direction was Thursday's fall.

Friday's gain still left the stock down 6.0% over twelve months, while the S&P 500 returned 9.8%. Over the past six months alone, Qualcomm lost 23.8%, while the S&P 500 gained 0.25%. At $165.41, the stock closed about a third below its highest close of the past twelve months, $251.02 on May 29, 2026. It remains well above its lowest close of the year, $124.07 on April 7, 2026.

The U.S. is currently home to 12 publicly listed companies worth $1 trillion or more. Semiconductor giant Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ: AMD) joined that exclusive club in September, but its stock has since declined by 25% from its peak, so the company is now valued at just $797 billion (as of the market close on Nov. 4).

AMD has become one of Nvidia's (NASDAQ: NVDA) top competitors in the market for data center graphics processing units (GPUs), which are the primary chips used in artificial intelligence (AI) workloads. Concerns about the sustainability of the AI infrastructure spending boom sparked the downside in AMD stock, but the company's operating results for the third quarter (ended Sept. 30) suggest sales won't be slowing down anytime soon.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Is this the ultimate buying opportunity for investors?

Image source: The Motley Fool.
Demand is soaring for AMD's data center chips

AMD launched its first dedicated AI data center GPU in 2023, and it was called the MI300X. It lagged Nvidia's original H100 GPU in terms of performance, but major tech companies like Microsoft, Meta Platforms, and Oracle thought it was a good alternative in the face of industrywide supply shortages.

AMD has since launched several new generations of its flagship GPU, and it has closed the gap to the competition. The company says its latest MI450 Series chips can be 15% more powerful and 30% more energy efficient than anything else on the market when installed in its fully integrated Helios data center rack. Helios includes specialized central processing units (CPUs), high-bandwidth memory, and networking components to extract the most processing power from every GPU.

AMD started shipping MI455X GPUs and Helios racks to a star-studded list of customers during the third quarter, which included Anthropic, OpenAI, Microsoft, Meta, and Oracle. OpenAI and Meta each plan to deploy 6 gigawatts' worth of computing capacity over the next few years using AMD's chips, and while they are starting with the MI450 Series, they will be big buyers of every future generation that follows.

In fact, AMD is already engaging customers regarding the MI500 Series and MI600 Series, which will deliver further leaps in performance.

AMD's third-quarter data center revenue nearly doubled

AMD generated $13.4 billion in revenue across its three core business segments during the third quarter, which was a 45% increase from the year-ago period. But the data center segment alone accounted for $8.5 billion of that total, and it grew by a whopping 97%.

Investors buy both NVIDIA (NVDA) and Micron Technology (MU) to capture the spending on AI data centers: NVIDIA sells the computing systems, and Micron sells DRAM and NAND memory. Micron trades at 9.2 times earnings compared with 23.4 for NVIDIA, making it look like the cheaper way in. Yet NVIDIA said in August that soaring memory prices had prompted a reset of its gross margin expectations. So will memory prices keep rising, and can NVIDIA keep growing while it pays them?

Are Memory Prices Still Rising For Micron?

They are, although Micron expects the increases to slow. During its August 26, 2026 call, NVIDIA said memory price increases had exceeded its expectations and were headed even higher. For NVIDIA, that serves as a cost warning, but for Micron, those same prices are what it sells at.

Micron provided a pricing outlook on its September 30 call. Management guided fiscal Q1 2027 revenue of $60 billion to $63 billion, compared with $54.2 billion in fiscal Q4 2026. That forecast assumes only single-digit growth in the bits of DRAM and NAND that Micron ships, leaving price and product mix to supply the rest of the rise.

Management also said price increases would continue at a more moderate pace. Micron's 86.0% guide for its gross margin sits just below the 86.8% it reported for fiscal Q4.

Can NVIDIA Keep Growing As Memory Costs Rise?

So far it can, although its margin is slipping. NVIDIA guided fiscal Q3 2027 revenue of $108 billion, plus or minus 2%, compared with $96.2 billion in fiscal Q2. Management expects fiscal 2028 revenue to grow about 70% and said supply, including of its new Vera Rubin systems, would remain the bottleneck through at least the end of that year.

The memory bill shows up in the margin instead. NVIDIA reported a 75.0% gross margin for fiscal Q2 and guided 74% for fiscal Q3, plus or minus half a point. Management expects it to bottom at 71% to 72% in fiscal Q4, then settle at 72% to 73% in fiscal 2028 as NVIDIA's own price increases take effect.

NVIDIA's margins have also been far steadier than those of Micron. NVIDIA's operating margin averaged 61.7% over the last three twelve-month periods, compared with 35.3% for Micron. Over those periods, NVIDIA's twelve-month operating margin stayed between 58.1% and 65.2%, while Micron's twelve-month operating margin climbed from 5.2% to 74.6% in two years.

How Do NVIDIA And Micron Compare Head To Head?

Over the latest twelve months, Micron comes out ahead on growth and margin. Micron's revenue grew 256.3%, against 83.4% for NVIDIA. Its operating margin was 74.6%, compared with 65.2% for NVIDIA. Each company has debt under 1% of its market value.
